summary: Gives the problem statement for the Interface to Network Security Functions work and some companion use cases. It sets out why a standard interface for managing security functions, such as firewalls, is needed.

eli5.summary: Different security guards speak different languages. This explains why it would be handy for them to share one language.

subtitle: A standard interface for controlling security functions from any vendor.

tldr.problem: Security service providers deploy firewalls, intrusion prevention systems, and other network security functions from many vendors, each with proprietary management interfaces, making it hard to automate control and monitoring.
tldr.mechanism: I2NSF defines a standard interface between security management systems and network security functions, allowing unified control regardless of which vendor's equipment is in use.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can mix security functions from different vendors and manage them through a single control interface, reducing cost and complexity.

facts.label: Number of interfaces
facts.value: 2 (Interface 1: client to controller; Interface 2: controller to NSF)

facts.label: Types of NSFs addressed
facts.value: Firewalls, IPS, IDS, DDoS protection, encryption, and others

today: RFC 8192 is an Informational RFC that establishes the problem statement and use cases for I2NSF. It has not been obsoleted. The IETF I2NSF working group continues to develop protocols and data models implementing the interface standards described in this document.

sections.title: Introduction to I2NSF
sections.content:
Interface to Network Security Functions (I2NSF) is a standard interface for controlling and monitoring network security functions. Network Security Functions (NSFs) are devices or software that protect networks, such as firewalls, intrusion detection systems, intrusion prevention systems, and DDoS mitigation tools.

Enterprises and service providers increasingly use a mix of security functions from different vendors. Some are deployed in their own data centers, while others are hosted by security service providers in the cloud. Without a standard interface, each NSF requires a different command format and control mechanism. I2NSF aims to solve this problem by defining a common way for management systems to control any NSF, regardless of vendor or location.
sections.eli5: Security tools need to be told what to do. Each tool speaks its own language, making it hard to give them orders. A standard language would help.

sections.title: The Problem: Diverse Security Functions and Interfaces
sections.content:
Organizations deploy many different types of security functions. A firewall protects against unwanted traffic, an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) stops known attacks, an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) logs suspicious activity, and DDoS protection mitigates distributed denial-of-service attacks. Some functions might sit at the edge of the network (a perimeter firewall), others in the data center (protecting virtual machines), and still others on customer networks (virtual security functions or vNSFs).

The challenge is that each vendor implements their security functions differently and provides different ways to control them. A firewall from Vendor A uses one command format, while a firewall from Vendor B uses another. Security administrators must learn each vendor's interface separately and write custom scripts to manage security policies across a heterogeneous environment. When a new vendor's tool is added, the entire integration must be rewritten. This complexity makes it expensive and slow to deploy new security functions.
sections.eli5: Each security tool has its own control panel and manual. Learning all of them is hard, and changing setup takes a long time because you have to update scripts for each tool.

sections.title: The I2NSF Architecture: Clients, Controllers, and Security Functions
sections.content:
I2NSF defines an architecture with three main entities. A Client requests security services (e.g., 'block all traffic to port 25 except from trusted servers'). This might be an application, a security management portal, or an automated orchestration system. A Security Controller receives these requests and translates them into commands that the underlying NSFs can execute. It also collects monitoring information from NSFs and reports it back to the client.

The Security Controller uses two interfaces. Interface 1 communicates with clients: receiving security requirements and returning monitoring data and statistics. Interface 2 communicates with NSFs: sending policy commands and collecting status information. By standardizing both interfaces, I2NSF allows any client to work with any controller, and any controller to work with any NSF. This decoupling is the key benefit: organizations can replace vendors or add new security functions without rewriting integration logic.
sections.eli5: A manager (the client) tells a coordinator (the security controller) what security is needed. The coordinator tells the guards (NSFs) what to do. A standard language between coordinator and guards makes everything work.

sections.title: Key Requirements and Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several critical requirements for I2NSF. First, it must provide a standard way to describe NSF capabilities. Not all security functions support all features—one firewall might support IPv6 filtering while another does not. The controller needs to know what each NSF can do. Second, I2NSF must support dynamic policy changes. When a DDoS attack occurs, the controller should be able to instantly modify rules without manual intervention.

Third, I2NSF must work with both traditional hardware-based NSFs and virtual NSFs (vNSFs) running on virtual machines that might be created, moved, or deleted. Fourth, it must support multi-tenancy: a service provider might manage NSFs for many customers simultaneously, each with different security policies. Fifth, I2NSF must allow NSFs to respond to external alerts (e.g., a DDoS detection system triggering automatic rule changes) and to receive updated threat signatures or profiles. Finally, it must provide secure key management: controllers need a standard way to distribute encryption keys and security credentials to distributed NSFs.
sections.eli5: The interface needs to let controllers ask 'what can you do?', change rules instantly, work with temporary guards (virtual NSFs), serve multiple customers, respond to alerts, and securely share passwords.

sections.title: Use Cases: From Access Networks to Data Centers
sections.content:
The RFC describes several practical use cases. In access networks, an Internet Service Provider manages virtual Customer Premises Equipment (vCPE) and virtual Provider Edge routers for thousands of customers, each with different security needs. Residential customers might need parental controls and malware protection, enterprise customers need flow-based security policies, and the provider needs to prevent DDoS attacks on its own infrastructure. I2NSF allows a single orchestration system to manage all of these.

In cloud data center scenarios, on-demand virtual firewalls are deployed when customers request them, then deleted when no longer needed. Security policies need to change instantly as workloads migrate between servers. DDoS and malware scenarios illustrate how I2NSF enables automatic responses: when a DDoS attack is detected, the controller automatically updates firewall rules to route attack traffic through a scrubbing service. Regulatory compliance scenarios show enterprises using I2NSF to ensure that policies are consistently enforced across on-premises and cloud-hosted security functions.
sections.eli5: Internet providers manage security for thousands of customers differently. Cloud systems spin up and tear down security tools instantly. DDoS attacks can trigger automatic responses. Compliance rules spread across multiple locations.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC acknowledges that I2NSF must be implemented securely. The interfaces must authenticate clients and controllers to prevent unauthorized changes to security policy. All communication between controllers and NSFs must be protected against eavesdropping and tampering, since policy commands and monitoring data can contain sensitive information. Controllers must ensure that NSFs are legitimate and have not been compromised, a concern especially important for virtual NSFs which may be created dynamically.
sections.eli5: Since the interface controls security, the interface itself must be secure. Only trusted managers should be able to give orders, and those orders should be encrypted so nobody can spy on them.
